contexts.context: The excerpt reports HIPS and PP FFF adhesion, not PEI, PPSU, PC, PEEK or PEKK. HIPS adhesion rose sharply near its Tg, with “pronounced increase” at 105°C attributed to improved wetting/interlocking; 110°C caused over-softening, creep, stress relaxation and variable, sometimes reduced strength. HIPS fracture width increased from 8.19 mm at 100°C to 13.47 mm at 110°C. PP widths increased from 7.23 mm at 80°C to 11.81 mm at 110°C, without significant adhesion-strength improvement. Detachment observations included HIPS on PEI sheet at 100–110°C; ULG and glass entries were unobserved.
contexts.question: Which quantitative studies measure first-layer adhesion (peel, shear or pull-off force) or warping of high-temperature thermoplastics printed by fused filament fabrication, such as polyetherimide (PEI/ULTEM), polysulfone/PPSU, polycarbonate, PEEK and PEKK, on different build platform materials (polyimide film, glass, PEI sheet, glass-fibre/epoxy, metal, coated or adhesive-treated surfaces), and how does the adhesion depend on bed temperature relative to the polymer's glass transition temperature? In particular, is there evidence that printing an amorphous polymer onto a bed made of the same polymer (for example ULTEM onto a PEI sheet) near or above its Tg causes interdiffusion or welding that makes the part hard or impossible to remove, and which release layers or surface choices prevent it?

contexts.context: The excerpt reports PLA and ABS, not PEI/ULTEM, PPSU, PC, PEEK or PEKK. Adhesion rose nonlinearly with bed temperature, peaking “slightly above the TG,” attributed to maximum segmental mobility. For PLA on PI, shear adhesion increased from 51±8 to 322±47 N; on glass, 73±19 to 651±17 N between 60–70°C (PLA Tg=60.6°C). ABS required PI and ≥120°C (above Tg) for large parts; ≥200 N was considered sufficient to resist warpage. Excessive adhesion (PLA/glass) could damage the bed; moderate temperatures or near-room-temperature cooling aided removal. No same-polymer welding/interdiffusion evidence is provided.

The original aluminium-clad PCB bed reached only 80 °C, whereas the upgraded 500 W silicone heater and aluminium plate reached a 200 °C peak and 150 °C continuous operating temperature. Initial PEI trials used a sanded carbon-fibre print surface; at a 150 °C bed and 365 °C nozzle, prints adhered well and showed no visible warping or shrinkage after cooling. However, thermal buckling of the aluminium bed caused approximately 1.5 mm of vertical edge deviation and uneven thickness. The revised build used slotted mounts and a 3 mm borosilicate-glass plate. contexts.context: The excerpt provides only a qualitative description of warpage in extrusion additive manufacturing. It states that warping is generally caused by non-uniform cooling, particularly when the bed temperature is too low for the material. The first layers shrink as they cool while upper layers remain hot and expanded, creating thermal stresses; insufficient adhesion to the build surface can then cause corners to curl and warping to occur. The supplied pages do not report quantitative measured warpage versus bed temperature, identify the exact print-surface plate material, state whether release film or glue was used, provide the glass-transition temperature (Tg) of PEI, document prints fused to a PEI build sheet, or specify the maximum achievable bed temperature. They do identify the material as polyetherimide (PEI), commercially called ULTEM, and describe it as a high-strength amorphous polymer with high temperature and chemical resistance. Information addressing the requested numerical measurements and machine/build-sheet details would need to be obtained from the full 2020 thesis and the 2022 Fabrizio publication, which are not included in this excerpt.

contexts.context: This excerpt discusses thermal control in the EFeSTO extrusion additive-manufacturing machine, but it does not provide the requested quantitative measurements of warpage versus bed temperature, exact print-surface plate materials, use of release film or glue, PEI glass-transition temperature (Tg), evidence of prints fused to a PEI build sheet, or a numerical limit for achievable bed temperature. It does state that bed-temperature uncertainty is a process problem because different materials require different temperatures for adhesion to the build surface. The excerpt emphasizes that operating temperatures must be established experimentally because machine geometry, thermal behavior, and material viscosity affect results. It also explains the central tradeoff in extrusion temperature: temperatures must be high enough to permit extrusion without overloading the motors, but not so high that the material degrades or becomes too soft for stable additive manufacturing. Thermal degradation may cause increased extrusion pressure or clogs. Separate cooling is required for motors, bearings, pistons, hopper components, and other machine parts that should remain near ambient temperature. The cited improvements involve using fan cooling or infrared preheating after extrusion to control the deposited material, but no bed-temperature data or warpage results are given here.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides general evidence that substrate or bed preheating can affect interlayer bonding and mechanical performance, but it does not contain the requested PEI/ULTEM-specific quantitative warpage-versus-bed-temperature measurements. It describes infrared heating experiments in which fracture energy increased with substrate heating until excessive intensity degraded the substrate surface; the effect also depended on printhead feed rate because faster movement reduced heating time. For ABS, infrared preheating had little effect when the initial substrate temperature remained above the material’s glass-transition temperature, but had considerable impact after the substrate cooled below Tg. A separate metal preheater produced greater necking, reduced void area, and approximately 60% higher tensile stress, attributed to increased bonding and diffusion. The excerpt does not identify the exact print-surface plate materials, whether release film or glue was used, the Tg of PEI, whether any prints fused to a PEI build sheet, or the maximum achievable bed temperature. It also does not report warpage values. The later machine description gives heater and safety details for the extrusion unit, including a thermal cutoff zone limited to 60 °C, but this is not identified as the build-bed temperature limit and should not be treated as such.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides indirect discussion of thermal interlayer bonding in PEEK40PEI60, rather than experimental evidence for high-temperature welding of a PEI/ULTEM interface made from the same polymer. It describes a diffusion-dominated regime at 150–180 °C, where suppressed crystallisation and retained chain mobility are associated with improved interlayer diffusion, entanglement, and ductility. Around 200 °C, partial crystallisation and continued diffusion produce a balance of stiffness and ductility. At approximately 230 °C, increased crystallisation restricts chain mobility and is associated with reduced interlayer bonding and brittle failure. However, the passage explicitly indicates that premature interfacial separation and the precise failure mechanism were not directly assessed. It does not report actual self-diffusion measurements, direct welding of PEI printed onto a PEI plate, a catastrophic unreleasable welded interface, or a time–temperature welding condition at a PEI glass-transition temperature near 217 °C. It also gives no glass-transition temperatures for ULTEM 9085 or ULTEM 1010. Therefore, the requested direct studies and Tg comparison cannot be identified from this excerpt.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides indirect experimental support for thermal welding or interlayer fusion of PEI through annealing above the glass-transition temperature. It states that heat treatment above Tg facilitates diffusion of PEI molecules across interfaces, increasing interlayer bonding and mechanical performance. The tested annealing temperatures were 220, 225, 230, and 235 °C, with the best overall mechanical results reported at 225 °C. Above 225 °C, thermal distortion and increasing brittleness degraded performance, although hardness continued to rise. The excerpt also links increased bonding to greater resistance during indentation and reports reduced fracture strain after annealing, consistent with increased stiffness and brittleness. However, it does not provide a direct measurement of molecular self-diffusion, a diffusion coefficient, weld healing kinetics, or a controlled time-temperature study at a specified Tg of approximately 217 °C. It also does not describe PEI/ULTEM 1010 printed directly onto a PEI plate, nor does it report a catastrophic or unreleasable welded interface. No comparison between ULTEM 9085 and ULTEM 1010 glass-transition temperatures is given. Thus, the passage supports the general mechanism of thermally enhanced PEI interlayer diffusion but cannot identify studies directly demonstrating the requested PEI-on-PEI-plate welding condition or provide Tg values for 9085 versus 1010.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides indirect evidence for thermally activated interlayer welding in a PEEK40PEI60 blend, rather than direct evidence for self-diffusion or catastrophic welding of PEI/ULTEM to an identical PEI plate. At 180 °C, near the glass transition of the PEI-rich phase, enhanced chain relaxation is described as promoting interdiffusion across layer interfaces while crystallisation remains suppressed; the material retains approximately 12% strain at break and reaches about 1750 MPa modulus and 109 MPa UTS. At 200 °C, the text identifies a narrow compromise window: limited crystallisation increases stiffness while sufficient chain mobility remains for effective interlayer diffusion. At 230 °C, greater crystallisation restricts chain entanglement and interlayer cohesion, producing high stiffness but reduced strength, ductility, and interlayer reliability. The cited evidence consists of tensile behavior, DSC, and XRD across top-layer temperatures from 150–230 °C. It does not report direct tracer-based self-diffusion measurements, PEI printed specifically onto a PEI/ULTEM plate, unreleasable interface testing, or Tg values for ULTEM 9085 versus 1010. The excerpt therefore cannot establish those requested material-specific comparisons.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes high-temperature FFF processing of PEI, but it does not provide the requested direct experimental evidence for thermal welding or molecular self-diffusion at a PEI/PEI interface. The excerpt does not report a PEI plate, an intentionally welded or catastrophic unreleasable interface, interface fracture testing, diffusion measurements, time-at-temperature studies, or fusion conditions near a glass-transition temperature of approximately 217 °C. contexts.context: This excerpt provides indirect experimental evidence relevant to thermal welding of PEI/ULTEM 1010 interfaces. It reports oven annealing at 220, 225, 230, and 235 °C, with 225 °C identified as particularly effective for improving interlayer adhesion. The authors attribute interlayer mechanical behavior to polymer diffusion bonding across the interface and state that annealing can enhance interfacial bonding and mechanical strength. The reported tensile, bending, and hardness improvements were approximately 10%, 5%, and 12%, respectively. However, the excerpt does not establish actual self-diffusion measurements, molecular interpenetration, or a time–temperature welding law. It also does not report a specimen printed directly onto a PEI plate, a catastrophic/unreleasable same-polymer weld, or a controlled comparison of interface fusion above versus below the glass-transition temperature. Although the question references Tg near 217 °C, this excerpt does not give a Tg value for either ULTEM 9085 or ULTEM 1010, nor does it compare those grades. It identifies ULTEM 1010 as amorphous, but provides no direct 9085-versus-1010 thermal-property data. Thus, the article supports annealing-assisted PEI interlayer adhesion at approximately 225 °C, while falling short of direct thermal-welding/self-diffusion evidence or the requested PEI-on-PEI plate experiment.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides indirect thermal-processing evidence relevant to PEI/ULTEM interfacial fusion, but it does not report a direct thermal-welding experiment. The authors state that annealing should be above the polymer’s glass-transition temperature and therefore tested 220, 225, 230, and 235 °C. These temperatures were selected as the usable range because visible profile distortion began above 235 °C; at 300 °C, PEI melted completely. FTIR showed that specimens annealed from 220–235 °C retained the basic PEI chemical structure, while XRD characterized the printed material as completely amorphous and found annealing-dependent changes in the broad peak/hump. Thus, the study supports thermal mobility, structural retention, and altered internal structure after annealing, but it does not demonstrate molecular self-diffusion across a PEI/PEI interface, quantify interlayer fusion at Tg, or document a catastrophic/unreleasable weld. The excerpt also contains no comparison of PEI 9085 versus ULTEM 1010 glass-transition temperatures and does not identify experiments specifically involving PEI printed onto a PEI plate. Those details would need to come from other studies or sections not included here.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides a practical high-temperature FFF report for PEI, rather than the full range of polymers listed in the question. The custom printer used an aluminium heated plate with a silicone heater; its continuous operating temperature was 150 °C, and PEI was printed with a 365 °C nozzle and 150 °C bed. Initial prints adhered well to a sanded carbon-fibre surface, but thermal buckling caused approximately 1.5 mm of edge deviation. The platform was subsequently changed to slotted mounts and 3 mm borosilicate glass. Because smooth glass did not provide sufficient adhesion by itself, the PEI manufacturer recommended PI tape (Kapton) plus PVP adhesive. The report states that the revised configuration had minimal warping and a 150 mm square printable area. It does not report cooling-release behavior, PEI self-welding, permanent sticking, or a quantitative adhesion-strength measurement. It also does not provide practical platform/release data for ULTEM 9085/1010, PC, PSU/PPSU, PEEK, PEKK, FR4/G10, or steel. Thus, the evidence distinguishes successful printing and qualitative adhesion from quantified adhesion, but cannot establish whether parts released on cooling.

contexts.context: This excerpt reports a quantified adhesion study for PETG, not for the high-temperature polymers listed in the question (ULTEM 9085/1010, PC, PSU/PPSU, PEEK, or PEKK). The tested platforms were pure aluminum, spring steel with PEI coating, tempered glass with a PI layer, and borosilicate glass. Twelve repeated measurements were made for each comparison, using maximum tear-off force as the adhesion metric. For the PI-coated tempered glass versus borosilicate glass comparison, the beds were printed at 85°C. The reported mean tear-off forces were 57.95 N for tempered glass with PI and 54.65 N for borosilicate glass; the authors characterize their adhesive properties for PETG as similar. For uncoated aluminum versus PEI-coated spring steel, the mean forces were 33.09 N and 53.48 N, respectively. The excerpt does not report printing ULTEM, PC, PSU/PPSU, PEEK, or PEKK; it does not establish an exact bed temperature for the aluminum/PEI comparison; and it provides no evidence about release on cooling, PEI self-welding, or permanent sticking. Thus, it distinguishes quantified PETG detachment forces from mere printing success, but cannot answer the requested high-temperature-polymer platform/release-layer question beyond these limited material comparisons.

contexts.context: This excerpt reports a quantitative primary study of additively manufactured PEEK, but it does not identify Lin (2024), report warpage, evaluate a square plate, compare bed/platform substrates, or provide a systematic heated-bed versus chamber comparison. The measured process variables were nozzle temperature, chamber temperature, and printing speed. Chamber temperature and printing speed most strongly affected crystallinity, while chamber and nozzle temperatures controlled mechanical behavior; printing speed affected inter- and intra-layer adhesion through the presence and size of voids. The strongest reported condition was a 440 °C nozzle temperature, 130 °C chamber temperature, and 2000 mm/min printing speed, producing approximately 89.3 MPa tensile strength, 3392.8 MPa Young’s modulus, and 30.9% crystallinity. Comparable performance above 87 MPa tensile strength and 3500 MPa modulus was obtained at 460 °C nozzle temperature with 130 °C chamber temperature and 1200 mm/min, or with 160 °C chamber temperature at 1200–2000 mm/min. Tensile strength above 80 MPa was associated with crystallinity above 29%. The excerpt discusses pores and crystallinity but gives no warpage measurements, glass-transition-temperature data, PEEK/CF composition, build-plate or substrate identity, or bed/platform material. Therefore, it can support process–structure–property comparisons for neat PEEK, but not the requested warpage/substrate study identification.

The abstract states that this setting reduced warpage through improved interlayer bonding. Tensile strength ranged from 45.36 to 71.4 MPa, while compressive strength ranged from 72.5 to 167 MPa. The 10% carbon-fiber PEEK composite had tensile strength 1.68 times that of pure PEEK. The introduction gives qualitative process guidance: higher bed temperatures improve adhesion and reduce thermal stress; nozzle temperature affects bonding and degradation; printing speed and environmental temperature/air circulation affect cooling gradients and warpage; and enclosed chambers with active heating can stabilize temperature. However, the excerpt supplies no chamber temperature, glass-transition-temperature (Tg) measurement, substrate identity, bed/platform comparison dataset, or direct dimensional warpage measurements.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the actual printed polymer as polyetherimide (PEI), not PPSU or PEEK. PEEK is mentioned only as a related super-engineering thermoplastic in the introduction, while PEI is the material experimentally studied. The reported PEI glass-transition temperature is approximately 177 °C. The heating method is in-situ infrared heating using a custom material-extrusion system with dual IR lamps positioned to maintain localized heating near the nozzle; the printed-layer surface was maintained above PEI’s Tg. Qualitatively, IR-assisted printing reduced warping and improved tensile strength, especially in the transverse direction. Increasing IR power also improved interlayer bonding and reduced voids, although excessive IR input slightly reduced longitudinal strength, indicating an optimum heating range. The provided excerpt does not give the quantitative warpage values or a numerical comparison between heated and unheated conditions. It also does not specify the build-plate surface or material, the bed temperature, or first-layer attachment results. Regarding bonding, it reports improved interlayer bonding in the printed part, supported by fractographic observations, but does not separately quantify first-layer adhesion to the build plate. Thus, only the polymer identity, Tg, IR-heating concept, and qualitative effects on warpage and interlayer bonding can be established from these pages.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Which quantitative studies measure first-layer adhesion (peel, shear or pull-off force) or warping of high-temperature thermoplastics printed by fused filament fabrication, such as polyetherimide (PEI/ULTEM), polysulfone/PPSU, polycarbonate, PEEK and PEKK, on different build platform materials (polyimide film, glass, PEI sheet, glass-fibre/epoxy, metal, coated or adhesive-treated surfaces), and how does the adhesion depend on bed temperature relative to the polymer's glass transition temperature? In particular, is there evidence that printing an amorphous polymer onto a bed made of the same polymer (for example ULTEM onto a PEI sheet) near or above its Tg causes interdiffusion or welding that makes the part hard or impossible to remove, and which release layers or surface choices prevent it?

## Scope and main finding

**Direct, quantitative measurements of adhesion *to the build plate* are much scarcer than measurements of interlayer strength or part warpage.** The retrieved plate-detachment studies test PLA/ABS, PETG, and HIPS/PP—not ULTEM, PPSU, PEEK, or PEKK. High-temperature-polymer studies do quantify warpage, and several document workable platform configurations, but they do not establish a peel or pull-off threshold at which ULTEM welds irreversibly to a PEI sheet. A *polyimide* (PI, often Kapton) film must not be confused with a *polyetherimide* (PEI, ULTEM) sheet. (spoerk2018effectofthe pages 3-4, kascak2024adhesiontestingdevice pages 8-9, santoso2025effectofbuild pages 2-5, vakharia2023multimaterialadditivemanufacturing pages 2-5)

### Quantitative evidence, with the measured interface identified

| Study | Printed polymer; surface and conditions | Actual measurement and result | Relevance and limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Spoerk et al. (2018)** | PLA or ABS on glass versus **PI film glued to glass**; bed 30–120 °C. Filament Tg: PLA **60.6 °C**, ABS **110.1 °C**. | Shear-off of individual printed strands: raising the bed **60→70 °C** increased PLA force **51 ± 8→322 ± 47 N on PI**, and **73 ± 19→651 ± 17 N on glass**. The study recommends PI and at least **120 °C** for sufficiently strong ABS attachment. At 70 °C, PLA adhesion could shear pieces from the glass; PI film remained largely intact. | Strong direct evidence that adhesion can rise abruptly as the *printed polymer* crosses Tg, and that excessive adhesion can damage a surface. **Neither PEI nor ULTEM was tested.** Forces depend on the strand geometry and shear-test protocol. (spoerk2018effectofthe pages 3-4, spoerk2018effectofthe pages 5-7, spoerk2018effectofthe pages 7-8) |
| **Kaščak et al. (2024)** | **PETG**, tested on PI-covered glass and bare borosilicate glass, both printed at **85 °C**; separately bare aluminium at **90 °C** and PEI-coated spring steel at **75 °C**. | Maximum tear-off force, 12 trials per surface: **PI 57.95 ± 5.70 N; glass 54.65 ± 12.10 N; aluminium 33.09 ± 5.52 N; PEI-coated steel 53.48 ± 7.95 N**. | Direct surface comparison, but **different bed temperatures** in the aluminium/PEI comparison prohibit assigning its entire force difference to surface chemistry. PETG is not ULTEM or another requested high-temperature feedstock. (kascak2024adhesiontestingdevice pages 8-9, kascak2024adhesiontestingdevice pages 9-11) |
| **Santoso et al. (2025)** | **HIPS** on PEI sheet, microporous-coated Ultrabed, or glass at **100, 105, 110 °C**; **PP** also attempted. HIPS Tg is described as approximately **95–105 °C**. | The paper measures build-plate detachment stress and reports its **maximum at 105 °C on PEI**, plotted in its *Figure 10*; the recoverable text does not give reliable exact point values. HIPS specimens could be formed on PEI but not on the tested coated bed or glass; PP lifted after roughly **2–3 layers** on the investigated surfaces. | Demonstrates a PEI-sheet/substrate comparison **for HIPS**, not PEI-on-PEI. Its separately plotted **interlayer** tensile stress must **not** be reported as bed-adhesion strength. Even the PEI/HIPS builds had later-layer formation difficulties. (santoso2025effectofbuild pages 2-5, santoso2025effectofbuild pages 8-10, santoso2025effectofbuild media dbdcd781) |
| **Adarsh and Nagamadhu (2025)** | **PEEK**, with 130, 140 or **150 °C** platform, **60 °C** chamber; other factors—nozzle, layer height, infill—also varied. The equipment specification calls its platform *ceramic glass*, whereas the methods call deposition onto a *carbon-fiber bed*: its actual exposed interface is consequently **ambiguous**. | Image-measured corner warpage of **100 × 30 × 5 mm** specimens: lowest mean **1.05 mm** at **130 °C** bed, 400 °C nozzle, 0.16 mm layer and 60% infill; highest **5.87 mm** at **150 °C** bed, 410 °C nozzle, 0.18 mm layer and 60% infill. | Quantitative **part warpage**, *not* plate-adhesion force. Because several settings change together, these runs do **not** establish that increasing the bed from 130 to 150 °C increases warpage or adhesion. (adarsh2025effectofprinting pages 2-4, adarsh2025effectofprinting pages 4-6, adarsh2025effectofprinting pages 11-14) |
| **Lee et al. (2026)** | **ULTEM 9085 PEI**, approximately **177 °C Tg in their report**; 370 °C nozzle, **80 °C chamber**, uncontrolled bed temperature, localized IR heating. Plate surface not specified. | Raising IR power **0→69 W** reduced measured transverse/longitudinal spring-back angles from approximately **8.1°/6.9° to 2.7°/2.4°**, respectively. | Quantitative **warpage**, and evidence that keeping deposited-layer interfaces hot improves *interlayer* bonding; **not** a comparison of build surfaces or measurement of first-layer release. Published estimates of 9085 Tg vary: Vakharia et al. give **186 °C** for their filament. (lee2026rapidpreheatingfor pages 6-11, lee2026rapidpreheatingfor pages 20-25, vakharia2023multimaterialadditivemanufacturing pages 2-5) |
| **Wu et al. (2014), Hu et al. (2019), Yang et al. (2021)**, as summarized by Lin (2024) | PEEK or short-CF/PEEK, varying **chamber** rather than platform surface. Wu: 150 °C fixed bed, **90–130 °C chamber**. Hu: 135 °C fixed bed, **25–60 °C chamber**. Yang: short-CF/PEEK, **20–200 °C chamber**. | Wu reported decreasing geometric warpage as chamber temperature rose. Hu reported warpage declining from **over 20% to 6.1%**, or **5.0%** using a local heat collector. Yang reported a *nonmonotonic* **0.2%→1.6%** as chamber rose **20→150 °C**, falling to **0.4% at 200 °C**. | These are **secondary-source summaries of primary experiments**, not independently inspected source datasets; they illustrate that chamber conditions and crystallization complicate any universal bed-Tg rule. The reported percentages are not comparable to Adarsh’s millimetres without common definitions. (lin2024processstructurepropertyrelationshipsof pages 21-26, lin2024processstructurepropertyrelationshipsof pages 155-157) |

**No directly verified quantitative first-layer peel, shear, or pull-off dataset was located for PC, PSU/PPSU, PEI/ULTEM, PEEK or PEKK across the requested PI/glass/PEI/G10–FR4/metal surfaces.** In particular, a reported peel force for a printed polymer–polymer *sandwich joint*, a part tensile strength, or a post-print coating pull-off test is not a build-plate detachment measurement. Similarly, Lin’s cited **4.4% PEEK versus 1.2% PEKK 70/30** thin-wall distortion data were *imported from another reference*, rather than measured as part of Lin’s own plate-material experiment. (lin2024processstructurepropertyrelationshipsof pages 39-42, adarsh2025effectofprinting pages 11-14)

## What temperature relative to Tg does—and does not—predict

Spoerk’s controlled first-layer study is the clearest experimental basis for the rule that heating a bed through the **deposited amorphous polymer’s Tg** can sharply improve contact and shear-off resistance. It also shows this is **not an assurance of easy release**: the hotter PLA–glass combination damaged glass. Conversely, its ABS adhered better to PI than glass, illustrating that surface chemistry and compliance matter alongside temperature. In Santoso’s different material pair, HIPS-on-PEI adhesion peaked near the **HIPS**, not the PEI-sheet, Tg. These results cannot be numerically extrapolated to ULTEM-on-PEI: the polymers, surface, contact time, part geometry, testing temperature, and failure mode change. (spoerk2018effectofthe pages 5-7, spoerk2018effectofthe pages 3-4, santoso2025effectofbuild pages 2-5, santoso2025effectofbuild pages 8-10)

**A hot nozzle is not the same as an entire PEI sheet being above Tg.** One ULTEM 9085 study reports filament Tg **186 °C** and prints on a **200 °C PVA-coated glass bed**; another reports an approximately **177 °C** Tg for its 9085 material. PEI/ULTEM 1010 annealing experiments use **220–235 °C** above that material’s Tg and find better interlayer properties, especially at **225 °C**. This supports the *plausibility* of chain mobility and interfacial welding when compatible PEI surfaces are held sufficiently hot, but neither experiment observes molecular diffusion across **ULTEM part–PEI build-sheet** interfaces or measures their removal force. Tg is a transition range, not a universal instantaneous welding threshold; the actual sheet-interface temperature, chain mobility, contact duration, grade compatibility and cooling history would have to be established. (vakharia2023multimaterialadditivemanufacturing pages 2-5, lee2026rapidpreheatingfor pages 6-11, yilmaz2022rheologycrystallinityand pages 1-2, yilmaz2022rheologycrystallinityand pages 3-4, yilmaz2022rheologycrystallinityand pages 6-7)

PEEK and PEKK require an additional qualification: their crystallization kinetics introduce shrinkage and may restrict chain motion. The contrasting PEEK/CF-PEEK chamber-warping trends above, and Lin’s discussion of slower-crystallizing PEKK, show why an amorphous-polymer bed-Tg adhesion rule should **not** be treated as a quantitative warpage or release law for these semicrystalline feedstocks. (lin2024processstructurepropertyrelationshipsof pages 21-26, lin2024processstructurepropertyrelationshipsof pages 39-42)

## Same-polymer welding and choices for a removable interface

**Conclusion on the specific hypothesis:** welding of hot, compatible PEI against PEI is **physically credible**, and published ULTEM interlayer annealing experiments support thermally enhanced bonding. **I did not find a controlled report showing that ULTEM printed onto a bare PEI sheet near/above its Tg becomes impossible to remove, nor a PEI-on-PEI plate peel-force measurement demonstrating that mechanism.** The HIPS-on-PEI data establish neither proposition; PI-film data are not PEI-sheet data. “Impossible to remove” should therefore be described as a *potential practical failure mode*, not a demonstrated threshold or established universal outcome. (yilmaz2022rheologycrystallinityand pages 1-2, yilmaz2022rheologycrystallinityand pages 6-7, santoso2025effectofbuild pages 8-10, spoerk2018effectofthe pages 3-4)

Documented ways of **avoiding direct contact with a bare PEI sheet** include:

* **Glass plus an intervening PVA coating/raft:** Vakharia et al. printed ULTEM 9085 and CF-9085 at a **200 °C bed** and **390 °C nozzle** on **PVA-coated glass**, using an ULTEM 9085 raft in the illustrated print. This documents *successful printing*, **not** quantified release on cooling or a guarantee against glass damage. (vakharia2023multimaterialadditivemanufacturing pages 2-5)
* **Glass covered with PI tape and PVP adhesive:** Shuttleworth’s PEI printing development used a **150 °C bed** and **365 °C nozzle**; after an aluminium platform buckled by about **1.5 mm**, it adopted **3 mm borosilicate glass** and manufacturer-advised **PI tape plus polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP)** for glass adhesion. This creates a non-PEI contact layer but was **not** tested as a controlled anti-welding or release-force comparison. (shuttleworth2020adigitalmanufacturing pages 71-75)
* **A different sacrificial/replaceable substrate:** Shuttleworth also reported successful small PEI prints on a **sanded carbon-fibre surface** at **150 °C**, without visible warping after removal and cooling; the study supplies neither a force measurement nor evidence that this surface is equivalent to glass-fibre/epoxy **G10/FR4**. Avoid treating those composites as interchangeable. (shuttleworth2020adigitalmanufacturing pages 71-75)
* **PEI sheet with an adhesion coating is *not* a demonstrated release solution:** Kothavade et al. found that a **different thermoplastic polyimide** would not reliably adhere to bare glass and instead printed at **130 °C** on a **PEI surface plus nano-polymer adhesive**. The printed resin was *not* ULTEM, its reported Tg was **245–250 °C**, and no PEI-on-PEI removal study was performed. An adhesive may increase hold-down; it should not be presumed to prevent permanent bonding unless its release behavior is tested. (kothavade2024extrusion3dprinting pages 2-4, kothavade2024extrusion3dprinting pages 4-5)

Thus, **a barrier or dissimilar, replaceable top surface is the defensible way to avoid intentionally printing PEI directly onto PEI**, while separately validating that the chosen PI tape, PVA/PVP coating, glass or composite plate both holds the specific print during cooling and releases it without substrate damage. The available examples establish process feasibility, not a comparative ranking of release forces for ULTEM, PC, PPSU, PEEK and PEKK; no experimentally validated release recommendation for bare G10/FR4 or metal across those feedstocks follows from these sources. (vakharia2023multimaterialadditivemanufacturing pages 2-5, shuttleworth2020adigitalmanufacturing pages 71-75, roschli2022buildplatedesign pages 3-7, spoerk2018effectofthe pages 7-8)

info.query: Which quantitative studies measure first-layer adhesion (peel, shear or pull-off force) or warping of high-temperature thermoplastics printed by fused filament fabrication, such as polyetherimide (PEI/ULTEM), polysulfone/PPSU, polycarbonate, PEEK and PEKK, on different build platform materials (polyimide film, glass, PEI sheet, glass-fibre/epoxy, metal, coated or adhesive-treated surfaces), and how does the adhesion depend on bed temperature relative to the polymer's glass transition temperature? In particular, is there evidence that printing an amorphous polymer onto a bed made of the same polymer (for example ULTEM onto a PEI sheet) near or above its Tg causes interdiffusion or welding that makes the part hard or impossible to remove, and which release layers or surface choices prevent it?
